numerical_failure.observed_behavior: With `KDEUnivariate(x).fit(fft=True, cut=0)`, the underlying `fast_linbin` binning mis-handles observations in the last bin (and the first two bins), producing incorrect bin counts; for the #9556 example the FFT density integrates to 0.8317 instead of ~1.0. Additionally, the original code could write out of bounds (touching `gcnts[M]`), causing a crash (malloc checksum error/abort).
numerical_failure.expected_behavior: The `fit` should run without crashing, and the FFT-based density should integrate to 1. For `fast_linbin`, bin counts should sum to the number of in-range observations (`nobs`) and match a reference linear binning (KernSmooth linbin) so that counts and moments are preserved.
trigger_conditions: `KDEUnivariate(endog).fit(fft=True, cut=0)` with some unique values; #9556 example uses `x = [24.0, 43.0, 27.0, 15.0, 37.0, 8.82]` (bad) and a related value `8.8` (good)
An observation falling in the last bin (`li == M - 1`), where the split `gcnts[li + 1] += rem` writes to `gcnts[M]` (out of bounds)
`cut=0` so the largest observation maps to `li == M - 1`; depending on rounding `rem` is a small nonzero number
With `trunc == 0`, a tail case adds to `gcnts[M]` directly (out of bounds)

Also in the original loop, observations with `li > 1 and li_i < M` meant observations in the first two bins were silently dropped; for the #9556 data the bin counts sum was 4.99999999999994 instead of 6

oracle_clues: Original behavior described as an out-of-bounds write when an observation falls in the last bin: for `li == M - 1` the split writes to `gcnts[M]` (one element past the end).

With `cut=0` the largest observation maps to `li == M - 1`, and depending on rounding `rem` can be a small nonzero number added just past a freed-or-live heap allocation; boundscheck builds raise `"Out of bounds on buffer access"`.

Counts correctness: “counts sum to nobs” and FFT density integrates to 1 within tolerance 0.01. The fix reports: counts sum changed from 4.99999999999994 to 6 and density integration from 0.8317 to 0.9979.

Numerical reference: rewrite matches KernSmooth linbin; on 200 random cases max abs difference of `1.1e-13` to reference, and counts sum correctly. (The passages mention this as a verification of the fix, not the buggy behavior.)

category_specific_evidence: KDEUnivariate(x).fit(fft=True, cut=0) crashes for some unique values of endog; example input x = [24.0, 43.0, 27.0, 15.0, 37.0, 8.82] triggers crash, while x = [24.0, 43.0, 27.0, 15.0, 37.0, 8.8] runs without crashing.

For the triggering array x = np.array([24.0, 43.0, 27.0, 15.0, 37.0, 8.82]), with a=x.min(), b=x.max(), and cut=0: lxi = (x - a) / ((b - a) / 511). The evidence states: “lxi[1] = 511.00000000000006  ->  li = 511 = M - 1, rem = 5.7e-14  ->  gcnts[512] += 5.7e-14”.

The diff explains the violated numerical boundary/grid assignment property: “X[i] == b, up to rounding in lxi; all of the weight belongs to the last grid point and gcnts[M] is out of bounds”, and adjusts logic so that when li_i >= M - 1, weight is accumulated into gcnts[M-1] instead of gcnts[M].
The fix rationale includes: “observations in [a, b] are split between the two enclosing grid points, an observation on the upper boundary is assigned to the last grid point”.

The issue-specific numerical artifacts include the concrete floating-point rounding rem = 5.7e-14 and lxi[1] = 511.00000000000006 (i.e., slight over 511 due to rounding), leading to out-of-bounds access gcnts[512] in the reported reproducer context.
reproduction_risks: Reproduction may fail or not crash depending on floating-point rounding behavior of lxi/li computations; evidence shows a specific near-boundary value lxi[1] = 511.00000000000006 causing rem = 5.7e-14 and an attempted update gcnts[512].
Using the “good” variant x ending in 8.8 instead of 8.82 may avoid the crash, so exact data values matter.

Crash trigger may depend on how unique values map to the FFT/bin grid through (x-a)/((b-a)/511), especially near the upper boundary X=b where rounding can make li hit M-1 and rem becomes a tiny positive value.
